prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of precision, opening new possibilities for tests of fundamental physics and measurement of time

statement.case_for: All eight of us put the optical lattice clock on our ballots, and half placed it in the top two or three, but I want to argue for it on scientific grounds and not on that count. The magic-wavelength idea is simple: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is the same for both clock levels, and the atoms can be held tightly without disturbing the transition. That removes Doppler and recoil effects while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. The consequence is fractional systematic uncertainty near 10^-18, confirmed by comparisons between independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST). That reproducibility is what I look for before I trust a result. The clocks have also turned into quantum many-body probes, with spin-polarised Fermi gases in lattices and the resolution of gravitational redshift across millimetres, and they have become a tool for fundamental-constant and dark-sector searches. It is precision atomic structure physics of exactly the kind where theory and experiment have to agree in every detail. The attribution is clean: Katori made the concept and the first lattice clocks, and Ye pushed the accuracy and stability to record levels and developed the many-body clock. The timing is good, since the 2012 prize covered ion control and cavity QED but not neutral-atom clocks.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a committee may read this as superb metrology and engineering refinement, and not as a discovery that reveals something unexpected about nature. It follows closely on the frequency comb prize (2005) and the ion-clock prize (2012), so novelty could be questioned. No fundamental-physics result has yet come out of the clocks, such as a variation of constants or a dark-matter signal, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Credit also extends beyond two names: Ye's JILA group colleagues, Lemonde at SYRTE, Takamoto and Hollberg all contributed, and I cannot weigh them reliably from memory. The ytterbium and aluminium-ion lineages are adjacent and not covered by the credited names.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks geometric and topological phases (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry) first as a unifying concept with a simple mechanism, and ranks the lattice clock only sixth, partly because of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I rank the Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase fifth myself, and it appeals to me exactly because it asks what the phase of a wavefunction means. I do not dismiss the concept. My difficulty is that it is nearly seventy years old in one half and forty in the other, and priority claims (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar) are real. Bohm is dead, so the pair would not represent the origin of the 1959 effect. On the overlap point I disagree. The comb and the ion-clock prizes were for tools and control of single ions. The lattice clock is a different principle, because many atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, and the lattice is what delivers the statistical power. The pending redefinition of the second would not change the discovery, though I accept that it may affect timing.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock fifth. She grants that the two-person split is fair and that performance is confirmed, but stresses the overlap with ion-clock work and the 2005 comb prize and whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second. She puts the aberration-corrected electron microscope first, as a genuine invention that made visible what could not be seen before.
responses.response: I take the aberration-correction case seriously as an invention with real impact, and it is a sound origin-of-the-tool argument for Rose, Haider and Krivanek. But I think it is weaker than the lattice clock on two points that matter in a physics prize. First, the results of the clock give a new quantitative probe of physics (gravitational redshift, constants), whereas an electron microscope is mainly a tool for other sciences, and the recent chemistry prize for cryo-EM may make the committee see it as chemistry or instrumentation. Second, I find the TEM versus STEM priority questions you raise make the attribution less clean than for Katori and Ye. On the 2005 and 2012 overlap I would say the same as to Mehlig: the underlying principle is different.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-led discovery that opened a new window, and ranks the lattice clock second. He is unsure about the credit among Halzen, Spiering and the collaboration, and about whether the diffuse flux or the source identification should be the prize.
responses.response: I largely defer to Pearce and Danielsson on astroparticle physics, and the diffuse flux is a real discovery where nature supplied the clue, which I value. My reservation is about attribution: you yourself say the credit is not clean, and a cubic-kilometre detector built by a large collaboration is hard to reduce to two names. The attribution for the lattice clock is simpler, and its confirmation is independent across many laboratories, while the neutrino sources are established only for a few objects. I would not oppose IceCube if the committee found a defensible attribution. If so, I would be interested to hear how you would define it, because the prize may need to be for the diffuse flux and not for the source identification.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as an enabling architecture behind superconducting processors, and notes that Wallraff, who did the first strong-coupling experiment, is not among the credited names. He also flags his own conflict because he works in this field.
responses.response: I agree with him that the missing name matters. I made the same observation on my own ballot, and with Wallraff absent I cannot support a prize from this credited list as the fairest outcome. I also doubt that circuit QED is sufficiently distinct so soon after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. The idea is elegant, and I know the atomic cavity QED it translates, but I would like to see a gap of some years first. I note that his declared conflict is appropriate and that I would count his scientific judgment on the coupling regime while discounting his ranking.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a discovery or as outstanding measurement science, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether other contributors (Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow and the wider JILA and SYRTE teams) have claims that would make a two-name credit unfair; I cannot verify this from memory.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second or for a first fundamental-physics result from the clocks.

Whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with the ultracold-atom quantum simulation (B001) would be stronger than either alone, and what the fair three-name subset for B001 is among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (Lund, 2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of the credited names on B013 (Katori, Ye) is a collaborator, so no specific recusal issue is apparent from my profile for my preferred configuration. My profile does not document any link with Katori or Ye. I work in theoretical atomic physics and my field is close to this one, which may colour my judgment.
